children: Proofpoint has agreed to acquire data-security company Varonis Systems for about $6.3 billion, as artificial-intelligence security continues to drive deals and investment across the cybersecurity industry.

Proofpoint will pay $49.75 a share in cash for Varonis, a 52% premium over the stock's June 22 closing price, the final trading day before reports of a potential sale first surfaced. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to approval from Varonis shareholders and regulatory bodies.

The acquisition comes as cybersecurity vendors scramble to expand their AI capabilities, both to defend against threats that use the technology and to safeguard corporate systems increasingly accessed by autonomous AI tools.

Varonis specializes in securing sensitive corporate data and managing access controls, while Proofpoint primarily focuses on email protection and user-level threat defense. The Wall Street Journal reported last month that the two firms were in advanced talks.

Proofpoint Chief Executive Sumit Dhawan said rapid enterprise AI adoption changes how organizations must protect their data. AI agents now frequently pull corporate information from traditional business software at speeds unimaginable just a few years ago, raising concerns over controls and safety.

Proofpoint evaluated building similar capabilities internally or forming a commercial partnership with Varonis, but Dhawan said management concluded it needed a full acquisition to respond effectively to AI-driven shifts.
"When the system has to work at machine speed, these signals need to have deep integration," Dhawan said. "We said, 'Look, this is only possible if we were working as a single team.'"

The transaction significantly expands Proofpoint's scale five years after private-equity firm Thoma Bravo took the company private in a $12.3 billion buyout. Dhawan said he believes the new platform approach ranks it among the top cybersecurity companies, and affirmed that Proofpoint continues to consider an eventual return to public markets.

"We do believe that the company is going to be very attractive for public investors from all the feedback we have heard, and the combination will only make it more attractive," he said. "We strategically are still thinking about going out into the public market."

Dhawan added that the Varonis acquisition largely rounds out the core platform Proofpoint aims to offer enterprise clients, though he didn't rule out targeted, smaller acquisitions to address future gaps.

The transaction reflects broader consolidation across the cybersecurity market as customers seek to streamline their vendor lists and buy integrated platforms, and cyber companies have continued to attract large investments and acquisition offers this year.

In June, Accenture agreed to spend about $4.2 billion for a majority stake in industrial cybersecurity company Dragos and acquisitions of runZero and NetRise, a deal that closed in September. Data-security company Cyera agreed in July to buy identity-security startup Oasis Security for $1 billion, while quantum-computing company IonQ struck a deal this month to acquire cybersecurity company Elisity for up to $1.3 billion.

"In the world of cybersecurity, you have oftentimes had 30 to 70, to sometimes even over 100 different vendors building out an architecture for an enterprise," Dhawan said. "That's just not sustainable."

Thoma Bravo is providing committed equity financing for the purchase and has secured debt-financing commitments. Institutional investor Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan will also acquire a stake in Proofpoint as part of the transaction.
Proofpoint and Varonis haven't yet determined whether Varonis will maintain its distinct brand after the transaction closes, Dhawan said.
